extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and policymakers interested in World War II military, diplomatic, and economic affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporary newspaper reporting and interpretive commentary on wartime policy, military strategy, logistics, censorship, and economic allocations during World War II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict censorship of communications with Axis-related countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Political defense of the hemisphere recommended that all American countries adopt strict censorship of all means of communications in the interests of continental safety; wording the recommendation to include such countries as Spain and Argentina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship is 'imperative over communications between American republics and any others keeping diplomatic relations with the Axis because diplomatic channels are the most important means of transmission.' The recommendation was framed as continental safety policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of communications to be censored (enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee specified classes of communications to be censored: (1) any to or from any of the Axis powers or occupied countries; (2) any non‑American nation not at war with the Axis; (3) any American country which has not broken relations with members of the Axis or has not yet banned communications with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three classes were listed explicitly as the scope for enforced censorship; the committee said the latter two classes would 'obviously' be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cuban sugar crop quota and allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuba's sugar crop was fixed at 3,225,000 short tons, of which 2,700,000 tons will be for sale to the United States, 300,000 tons for export to other countries, and 225,000 tons for domestic consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The allocation was decreed under presidential authority; production in recent years has been limited by presidential decree and prior quotas are cited for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of auxiliary police ('rural guards') to assist overburdened police
rubrics_metrics.description: An auxiliary police organization of 'rural guards' was formed in Germany to assist regular police overburdened by wartime duties; similar 'city guards' were to be formed in German cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Daluege disclosed these auxiliaries have men 40 to 60 years old serving as policemen in their spare time; they are businessmen, peasants, industrialists or workers doing police duty 'in their spare time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat enemy/broadcast claims as unconfirmed unless corroborated
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese claims (e.g., of Allied ships and planes sunk) were reported in broadcasts but were explicitly noted as 'not confirmed by any other source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report records such enemy claims but cautions readers that these claims lack independent confirmation; reporting distinguishes recorded enemy broadcasts from verified facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified command and apportionment of forces (Allied operational plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United Nations' plan for action comprises 'apportionment of forces as well as their direction and weight'; Allied command in North Africa was unified under American command (Gen. Eisenhower), with apportionment and direction planned for the next nine months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece reports appointments (Eisenhower as supreme commander, Alexander as deputy, Tedder for air support, etc.) and emphasizes that the Allies 'have a complete plan of action' and will meet again to finalize details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority to anti‑U‑boat warfare and shipping protection
rubrics_metrics.description: U‑boat warfare takes first place in Allied considerations; the protection of shipping (convoys, escorts, long‑distance aircraft) is prioritized as essential before large-scale land operations abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Churchill emphasized that the U‑boat problem must be met first; well‑escorted convoys, especially when protected by long‑distance aircraft, greatly mitigate losses. The article cites lower losses in heavily‑escorted troop convoys as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize production of escort vessels even if it impinges on newbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Decided to place greater emphasis on producing escort vessels, even though that may impinge on new merchant shipbuilding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large numbers of escort vessels are being constructed in Britain and the U.S., equipped with the latest anti‑U‑boat devices; resources are pooled with the United States and fair allocation of American-built escorts is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer fast ships when optimal but balance speed versus aggregate tonnage
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast ships are preferable ('every one sees how much better it is to have fast ships than slow') but speed is costly and introduces trade-offs in engines and materials; choices between fewer fast ships or more slow ones require careful calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should aim at the 'optimum' rather than the maximum; engine competition and material allocation complicate moving to faster vessels even if tactically desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold exact loss figures publicly to deny enemy intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable to leave the enemy guessing at real figures and not to publish exact figures of losses, to prevent the enemy from checking exaggerations or associating particular losses with particular operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Churchill deliberately gave no specific figures in speech to keep the enemy uncertain; the policy is presented as operational security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflexible insistence on unconditional surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: The Allies reaffirmed an inflexible insistence on unconditional surrender as a principal war aim (though discussion included whether to embody it in treaties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Churchill discussed unconditional surrender as a dominating aim set at Casablanca; the article notes this stance while also describing related diplomatic offers and considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess battle significance by strategic and moral effects, not just scale
rubrics_metrics.description: A battle's importance should be judged by its strategic and moral effects rather than strictly by its physical size or numbers; Guadalcanal, though small, is likened to Belleau Wood for its lasting meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive commentary argues local actions can have meaning far beyond square mileage or enemy numbers annihilated; moral effects may influence the course of the war.
